key_insight: Translation symmetries in language co-occurrence statistics impose strong constraints on learned representations, causing simple geometric structures (e.g., circles for months, smooth 1D manifolds for years, linearly decodeable spatial coordinates) to emerge naturally in model embedding space.
problem_solved: Explains why pretrained language models develop crisp, low-dimensional geometric organization in their representations despite complex training dynamics—linking observable geometric phenomena to concrete statistical symmetries in language data.
method: Theoretical analysis: derive how a translation symmetry in token co-occurrence probabilities constrains the space of optimal representations.
Empirical validation: probe multiple models and corpora with linear decoders, PCA and manifold visualizations to recover circles, 1D manifolds, and linearly-decodable coordinates.
Controlled experiments: synthetic data and ablations that add/remove symmetry to demonstrate causality between statistical symmetry and emergent geometry.
impact: Provides a principled explanation for common geometric patterns in LLM representations, improving interpretability and informing better probing, diagnostics, and dataset or architecture choices that exploit or avoid such symmetries.
visual_elements: Token-token co-occurrence heatmap showing a translation-invariant pattern (visual cue for symmetry).
Embedding-space schematic: labeled points arranged on a circle (months) and a smooth 1D curve (years) to illustrate emergent geometry.
Scatterplots with linear-probe fits decoding latitude/longitude and month labels from embeddings.
Pipeline flow: dataset symmetry → theoretical constraint → model training → empirical probes/ablations (showing causal link).
paper_title: Symmetry in language statistics shapes the geometry of model representations
paper_authors: Dhruva Karkada, Daniel J. Korchinski, Andres Nava, Matthieu Wyart, Yasaman Bahri
